l: threshing floor, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 3
s: The threshing floor is where Boaz winnows barley on the night in question. He lies down at the end of the heap of grain there, and Ruth comes softly and lies at his feet. Boaz asks that it not be known that a woman came to the threshing floor, and Ruth leaves there before dawn.

l: kinsman's duty, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 3
s: Ruth appeals to Boaz as a near kinsman, and he affirms that he is one but that a nearer kinsman has the first claim. Boaz says that if the nearer kinsman performs the duty, good, but if he will not, Boaz will do it, swearing by the LORD's life. Naomi expects Boaz to settle the matter that same day.

l: The Book of Ruth, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 4
s: Boaz goes to the city gate, calls the near kinsman over, and gathers ten elders as witnesses. He tells the kinsman that Naomi is selling Elimelech's parcel of land and that Ruth the Moabitess must also be acquired with it to raise up the name of the dead. The kinsman at first agrees to redeem the land but then declines, fearing he would endanger his own inheritance, and confirms the transfer by taking off his sandal. Boaz declares before the elders and people that he has bought all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion and Mahlon and has purchased Ruth to be his wife. The people bless him, Ruth conceives and bears a son, the women praise the LORD with Naomi, who nurses the child, and he is named Obed, father of Jesse and grandfather of David, followed by the generations from Perez to David.

l: Boaz, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 4
s: Boaz sits at the gate, summons the near kinsman and ten elders, and offers the kinsman the chance to redeem Elimelech's land. When the kinsman refuses, Boaz takes the right of redemption, declares before the witnesses that he has bought all that was Elimelech's, Chilion's and Mahlon's and has purchased Ruth to be his wife. He marries Ruth, and he is named in the genealogy as the son of Salmon and father of Obed.

l: near kinsman (of Boaz and Elimelech's family), The Book of Ruth, Chapter 4
s: The near kinsman comes to the gate at Boaz's call and first says he will redeem the land, but after Boaz adds that he must also buy it from Ruth, he says he cannot lest he endanger his own inheritance. He gives Boaz his right of redemption and takes off his sandal to formalize the transaction.

l: Naomi, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 4
s: Naomi, who has come back from Moab, is the one selling the parcel that was Elimelech's, and Boaz buys it from her hand. After Ruth's son is born, the women bless the LORD for giving her a restorer of life, and Naomi takes the child to her bosom and becomes his nurse. The neighbor women say "A son is born to Naomi."

l: Ruth, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 4
s: Ruth the Moabitess, wife of Mahlon, is named by Boaz as something that must be bought along with the field to raise up the name of the dead. Boaz purchases her to be his wife, the LORD enables her to conceive, and she bears a son. The women say she loves Naomi and is better to her than seven sons.

l: Obed, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 4
s: Obed is the son born to Boaz and Ruth, and the women declare he will be a restorer of life and sustainer of Naomi in her old age. The neighbor women name him Obed, and the text identifies him as the father of Jesse, the father of David.

l: parcel of land (Elimelech's field), The Book of Ruth, Chapter 4
s: The parcel that was Elimelech's is being sold by Naomi, and Boaz offers it first to the nearer kinsman before the elders. The kinsman declines to redeem it, and Boaz buys it, along with all that was Elimelech's, Chilion's and Mahlon's.

l: redemption of the land and Ruth, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 4
s: Boaz offers the redemption first to the near kinsman, who agrees to the land but backs out once he learns it includes buying Ruth to raise up the name of the dead on his inheritance. The transfer is formalized by the sandal custom, and Boaz declares before the elders and people that he has bought the land and purchased Ruth so the dead man's name will not be cut off. The people answer "We are witnesses" and bless the arrangement.

1 Chronicles 1 opens a genealogy running from Adam through Seth, Enosh and the line down to Noah, whose sons are Shem, Ham, and Japheth. It lists the descendants of Japheth, Ham (including Cush, who fathered Nimrod, and Mizraim, from whom the Philistines came), and Shem down through Arpachshad, Eber, Peleg and Joktan to Abram, also called Abraham. It then lists Abraham's sons Isaac and Ishmael, the sons of Ishmael, and the sons of Keturah, Abraham's concubine. Isaac's sons Esau and Israel are named, followed by Esau's descendants and the sons of Seir. The chapter ends with the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel and the chiefs of Edom.
Adam is named first in the genealogy, heading the line that runs through Seth and Enosh down to Noah.
Noah is listed in the line from Adam as the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth, from whom the following lists of descendants are traced.

Shem's sons are listed as Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, Aram, Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech. The line through Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor and Terah leads to Abram, also called Abraham.

Ham's sons are given as Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan, and their descendants are listed. Cush became the father of Nimrod, who began to be a mighty one on the earth, and Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn along with several peoples.
Japheth's sons are listed as Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer and of Javan are also named.
Abraham, also called Abram, is the end of the line from Shem through Terah. His sons Isaac and Ishmael are named, and he also had sons by Keturah, his concubine.
Isaac is named as a son of Abraham, and Abraham became his father. Isaac's sons are Esau and Israel.
Ishmael is named as a son of Abraham, and his sons are listed with Nebaioth as firstborn, followed by Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, and others, twelve in all.
Esau is named as a son of Isaac, along with Israel. His sons are Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah, and the descendants of Eliphaz and Reuel are listed.
Edom is described as a land where kings reigned before any king reigned over the children of Israel. The chapter closes with a list of its chiefs.

l: kings of Edom, 1 Chronicles, 1 Chronicles / Chapter 1
s: The kings who reigned in Edom were Bela son of Beor, Jobab son of Zerah, Husham, Hadad son of Bedad, Samlah, Shaul, Baal Hanan son of Achbor, and a later Hadad. Each reigned in place of the one who died, and the last Hadad's wife was Mehetabel.

l: chiefs of Edom, 1 Chronicles, 1 Chronicles / Chapter 1
s: After Hadad died, the chiefs of Edom are listed as Timna, Aliah, Jetheth, Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, Magdiel, and Iram.

Chapter 2 lists the twelve sons of Israel and then concentrates on the descendants of Judah. Judah's sons Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez and Zerah are named, with Er killed for wickedness and Tamar bearing Perez and Zerah. The line of Hezron is traced through Ram to Jesse and his seven sons, ending with David, along with Jesse's daughters Zeruiah and Abigail and their children. The chapter then gives the branches of Hezron's sons Jerahmeel and Caleb, including Sheshan's daughters and his Egyptian servant Jarha, and closes with Caleb's descendants and the families tied to Kiriath Jearim, Bethlehem and the scribes at Jabez.

Judah had sons Er, Onan and Shelah by Shua's daughter, and Perez and Zerah by his daughter-in-law Tamar, five sons in all. Er, his firstborn, was wicked in the LORD's sight and was killed. Judah's descendants through Perez and Zerah form the main line of the chapter.

Hezron, a son of Perez, fathered Jerahmeel, Ram and Chelubai. At sixty he took the daughter of Machir as wife, and she bore him Segub. After he died in Caleb Ephrathah, his wife Abijah bore him Ashhur the father of Tekoa.

Jerahmeel was Hezron's firstborn, and his sons were Ram, Bunah, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah. He had another wife, Atarah, who was the mother of Onam. His line includes Onam's descendants and Sheshan's line, and his brother was Caleb.

Caleb, son of Hezron, had children by Azubah and Jerioth, and after Azubah died he married Ephrath, who bore Hur. His concubines Ephah and Maacah bore further sons, and his daughter was Achsah. His line through Hur includes Shobal, Salma and Hareph, linked to Kiriath Jearim, Bethlehem and Beth Gader.

Ram, a son of Hezron, became the father of Amminadab, beginning the line through Nahshon, Salma, Boaz, Obed and Jesse to David. A different Ram was the firstborn of Jerahmeel, whose sons were Maaz, Jamin and Eker.
David is named as the seventh son of Jesse, in the line from Ram through Amminadab, Nahshon, Salma, Boaz and Obed. His sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail.

Sheshan, a descendant of Jerahmeel through Appaim and Ishi, had no sons, only daughters. He gave a daughter as wife to his Egyptian servant Jarha, and she bore Attai, who began a line running through Nathan and others to Elishama.
The twelve sons of Israel are listed: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad and Asher. The chapter then turns to Judah's descendants.

Chapter 3 lists the descendants of David. It first names the six sons born to him in Hebron, where he reigned seven years and six months, and then the sons born in Jerusalem, where he reigned thirty-three years, including Solomon by Bathshua. It then traces the royal line from Solomon through Rehoboam down to Josiah, and names Josiah's four sons. Finally it follows the line through Jehoiakim and Jeconiah the captive, then Pedaiah and Zerubbabel, and on to later generations ending with the seven sons of Elioenai.

David had six sons born to him in Hebron, beginning with Amnon, and four sons by Bathshua plus others in Jerusalem, for nine listed there. He reigned seven years and six months in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. The text also notes he had sons of concubines and that Tamar was their sister.
Hebron is where six sons were born to David: Amnon, Daniel, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah, and Ithream. David reigned there seven years and six months.
Jerusalem is where David reigned thirty-three years. Nine sons were born to him there, including Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon, the first four by Bathshua daughter of Ammiel.
Solomon is listed as one of four sons born to David in Jerusalem by Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel. His son was Rehoboam, who begins the line of succeeding kings.
Rehoboam is named as Solomon's son. He heads the list of royal descendants, followed by Abijah his son, then Asa and Jehoshaphat.
Josiah appears at the end of the royal succession as the son of Amon. His sons were Johanan the firstborn, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, and Shallum.
Jeconiah is listed as a son of Jehoiakim and is called the captive. His sons were Shealtiel, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah.
Zerubbabel is named as a son of Pedaiah, together with Shimei. His sons were Meshullam and Hananiah, and Shelomith was their sister, with five more children listed after them.

Chapter 4 continues the genealogies of the sons of Judah, listing descendants of Perez, Hur, Ashhur, Kenaz, Caleb, Ezrah and Shelah, including various families of Zorathites, craftsmen, potters and linen workers. It pauses to note Jabez, who was more honorable than his brothers and whose prayer for blessing and protection God granted. The chapter then lists the sons of Simeon and their descendants, noting that Shimei had many children but the family did not multiply like Judah. It names the cities where Simeon's families lived until David's reign. In the days of Hezekiah, princes of Simeon's families found good pasture near Gedor and destroyed the Meunim there, and five hundred Simeonites went to Mount Seir and struck the remnant of the Amalekites.

Judah's sons are listed as Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal, and many descendant families are traced from them, including Zorathites, craftsmen, and potters. His son Shelah's line is also recorded. The Simeonites are said not to have multiplied like the children of Judah.

Jabez was more honorable than his brothers, and his mother named him Jabez because she bore him with sorrow. He called on the God of Israel to bless him, enlarge his border, be with him, and keep him from evil so that he would not cause pain. God granted what he requested.
God is called the God of Israel by Jabez, who asks for blessing, an enlarged border, his protecting hand, and deliverance from evil. God granted Jabez what he requested.

Simeon's sons are listed as Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul, with descent traced through Shallum, Mibsam, Mishma, and onward. Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters, but the family did not multiply like Judah. They lived in cities such as Beersheba, Moladah, and Ziklag until David's reign, and kept their genealogy.

Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah, Joel, Jehu, Elioenai, Ziza, and others named are called princes in their families, whose fathers' houses increased greatly. They went to the entrance of Gedor to seek pasture, found it rich and peaceful, and in Hezekiah's days struck the tents and the Meunim there, destroying them utterly and settling in their place.

l: Simeonite expedition to Mount Seir, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 4
s: Five hundred men of the sons of Simeon went to Mount Seir under the captains Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, sons of Ishi. They struck the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped and have lived there to this day.

Chapter 5 records the genealogy of Reuben, Israel's firstborn, whose birthright passed to Joseph's sons because he defiled his father's couch, while Judah prevailed and produced the prince. It lists Reuben's sons and the line of Joel down to Beerah, whom Tilgath Pilneser of Assyria carried away captive, and it names the Gadites living in Bashan. In the days of Saul and later, Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh fought the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab, crying to God and trusting him, and they took vast plunder in livestock and men. The half-tribe of Manasseh grew from Bashan to Mount Hermon and listed its mighty heads of houses, but they trespassed against God by following the gods of the land's peoples. God therefore stirred up Pul and Tilgath Pilneser, kings of Assyria, who carried the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan.

Reuben is identified as the firstborn of Israel who lost his birthright to the sons of Joseph because he defiled his father's couch. His genealogy is therefore not listed according to the birthright, and his sons are named as Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.

The sons of Reuben are Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi, with a line through Joel to Beerah, the prince of the Reubenites. They lived from Aroer to Nebo and Baal Meon and eastward toward the Euphrates because their livestock multiplied in Gilead. They fought the Hagrites with the Gadites and half-tribe of Manasseh, and were later carried away by Assyria.
Beerah is the son of Baal in the line of Joel and was prince of the Reubenites. Tilgath Pilneser king of Assyria carried him away captive.

Tilgath Pilneser, king of Assyria, carried Beerah the Reubenite prince away captive. God stirred up his spirit, and he carried the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan.

The Hagrites were fought in the days of Saul and fell by the hand of the Reubenites, who lived in their tents east of Gilead. In a later war, with Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab, they were delivered into the hands of Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh, who took their camels, sheep, donkeys, and men.

The Gadites lived beside the Reubenites in Bashan to Salecah, and their chiefs included Joel, Shapham, Janai, and Shaphat, along with kinsmen of their fathers' houses. They were listed by genealogy in the days of Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam of Israel. They joined the war against the Hagrites and were later carried into exile by the Assyrian kings.

The half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land and increased from Bashan to Baal Hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon, with seven named heads of fathers' houses described as mighty men of valor. They joined the war against the Hagrites, then trespassed against the God of their fathers by following the gods of the land's peoples. For this they were carried away to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan.

God helped Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh against the Hagrites, answering them because they cried out and trusted him, and the war was of God. After they trespassed against him, the God of Israel stirred up the spirits of Pul and Tilgath Pilneser to carry them into exile.
Pul is a king of Assyria whose spirit the God of Israel stirred up. He is named together with Tilgath Pilneser in the carrying away of the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh.

l: war against the Hagrites, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, with 44,760 valiant men able to go to war, fought the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. They were helped because they cried to God and trusted him, and the enemy fell into their hands. They took 50,000 camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys, and 100,000 men, and lived in their place until the captivity.

God stirred up Pul and Tilgath Pilneser, kings of Assyria, who carried the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh away. They were brought to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan, where they remain to this day.

l: idolatry (trespass of Manasseh half-tribe), 1 Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: The heads of the half-tribe of Manasseh trespassed against the God of their fathers and played the prostitute after the gods of the peoples of the land whom God had destroyed before them. This unfaithfulness precedes God's stirring up of the Assyrian kings to carry them into exile.

Chapter 6 lists the descendants of Levi through his sons Gershom (Gershon), Kohath, and Merari, tracing the high-priestly line from Aaron's son Eleazar down to Jehozadak, who went into captivity under Nebuchadnezzar. It names the Levites whom David set over the service of song after the ark came to rest, with Heman of the Kohathites, Asaph of the Gershomites, and Ethan of the Merarites. It says Aaron and his sons made offerings and atonement for Israel as Moses commanded, while the other Levites served the tabernacle. The chapter ends by listing the cities and pasture lands given by lot to the Aaronite priests and the Kohathite, Gershomite, and Merarite families from the tribes of Israel.
Levi is named as the father of Gershom (Gershon), Kohath, and Merari. The genealogies of the singers Heman, Asaph, and Ethan all trace back to him, and Heman's line goes further back to Israel.

Gershom is listed as a son of Levi, with sons Libni and Shimei, and a line running through Libni, Jahath, Zimmah, Joah, Iddo, Zerah, and Jeatherai. Asaph's ancestry runs back through Gershom to Levi. The sons of Gershom received thirteen cities from Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Manasseh in Bashan.

Kohath is listed as a son of Levi, with sons Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Aaron's priestly line and Heman the singer both descend from him. Kohath's families received cities by lot, including thirteen for Aaron's sons and ten more for the rest of the Kohathites.

Merari is listed as a son of Levi, with sons Mahli and Mushi. Ethan, who stood on the left hand in the service of song, descends from him. The sons of Merari received twelve cities by lot from Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun.

Aaron is named as a child of Amram, with siblings Moses and Miriam, and as the father of Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. He and his sons offered on the altars and made atonement for Israel as Moses, the servant of God, had commanded.
David is said to have set the singers over the service of song in the LORD's house after the ark came to rest there. They served before the tabernacle until Solomon built the house in Jerusalem.

Heman the singer is identified as a Kohathite, the son of Joel and the son of Samuel. His ancestry is traced back through Elkanah, Korah, Izhar, Kohath, and Levi to Israel. He served in the song ministry alongside his brother Asaph.

Asaph, the son of Berechiah, is called Heman's brother and is said to have stood on his right hand in the service of song. His ancestry is traced through Shimea, Zerah, Jahath, and Gershom back to Levi.

Ethan the son of Kishi is a Merarite who served in the song ministry on the left hand, standing among the brothers of Heman and Asaph. His ancestry is traced through Abdi, Malluch, Mahli, Mushi, and Merari to Levi.

The Levites are the descendants of Levi through Gershom, Kohath, and Merari. Those who were not priests were appointed to all the service of the tabernacle of God's house. The children of Israel gave them cities with pasture lands by lot.

The sons of Aaron are named as Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. The line through Eleazar continues to Phinehas, Zadok, Ahimaaz, and later priests down to Jehozadak. They received thirteen cities from Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin, including Hebron, which was the Kohathites' first lot.

l: Levite cities with pasture lands, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 6
s: The cities with pasture lands were given to the Levites by lot from across the tribes. Thirteen went to Aaron's sons, ten to the rest of the Kohathites, thirteen to the Gershomites, and twelve to the Merarites. The fields and villages of Hebron went to Caleb the son of Jephunneh.

l: service of song (David's appointed singers), 1 Chronicles, Chapter 6
s: David set the singers over the service of song after the ark came to rest. Heman the Kohathite, Asaph the Gershomite, and Ethan the Merarite served in order, with Asaph on Heman's right and the Merarites on the left. They ministered before the tabernacle until Solomon built the LORD's house in Jerusalem.

Chapter 7 gives genealogies and military counts for several tribes. It lists the sons of Issachar (Tola, Puah, Jashub, Shimron), the sons of Benjamin (Bela, Becher, Jediael), and brief entries for Naphtali. It then covers Manasseh's line through Machir and Gilead, and Ephraim's line, including the killing of his sons by the men of Gath, the birth of Beriah, his daughter Sheerah's building of towns, and the descent down to Joshua. The chapter lists the territories where Joseph's children lived and closes with the sons of Asher and a count of twenty-six thousand men for war.

Issachar's sons are named as Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron, four in all. His families included mighty men of valor, listed by genealogy as eighty-seven thousand, and bands of the army numbered thirty-six thousand because they had many wives and sons.
Tola's sons were Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their fathers' houses and mighty men of valor. Their number in the days of David was twenty-two thousand six hundred.

Benjamin's sons are listed as Bela, Becher, and Jediael. Bela's line was counted at twenty-two thousand thirty-four, Becher's at twenty thousand two hundred, and Jediael's at seventeen thousand two hundred, all mighty men of valor able to go out to war.

Manasseh's son Asriel was born to his concubine the Aramitess, who also bore Machir the father of Gilead. The chapter traces his descendants through Machir and Gilead, and the children of Manasseh share borders with Joseph's children's settlements.

Machir, father of Gilead and son of Manasseh, took a wife of Huppim and Shuppim whose sister was named Maacah. Maacah, the wife of Machir, bore Peresh, and the line continues through Peresh's brother Sheresh and his sons Ulam and Rakem.

Ephraim's sons are traced through Shuthelah, Bered, Tahath, and others. Two of them, Ezer and Elead, were killed by the men of Gath when they came down to take livestock, and Ephraim mourned many days while his brothers came to comfort him. His line is followed down to Nun and Joshua, and his children lived in Bethel, Gezer, Shechem, and other listed places.
Beriah was born to Ephraim and his wife after Ephraim went in to her following the deaths of his sons. He was named Beriah because there was trouble with Ephraim's house.
Sheerah was the daughter of Ephraim's house in the line of Beriah. She built Beth Horon the lower and the upper, and Uzzen Sheerah.

Asher's sons were Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, and Beriah, and Serah was their sister. His descendants, through Beriah, Heber, Japhlet, Shemer, Helem, and others, are listed as heads of fathers' houses and choice mighty men of valor, numbering twenty-six thousand men for war.

Chapter 8 gives genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin. It begins with Benjamin's five sons and the sons of Bela, then lists the heads of households of Geba and the descendants of Shaharaim, including the sons of Elpaal, Beriah, Shimei, and Shashak, who lived in Jerusalem. It then names the family of the father of Gibeon, who lived in Gibeon and Jerusalem. The chapter traces Ner to Kish to Saul and Saul's sons, continues through Jonathan's son Merib-baal down to Azel's six sons and the sons of Eshek, and ends by noting that Ulam's sons were mighty archers with 150 sons and grandsons.

Benjamin became the father of Bela his firstborn, Ashbel, Aharah, Nohah, and Rapha. The chapter closes by saying that all the listed descendants, including Ulam's many archer sons and grandsons, were of the sons of Benjamin.
Bela is named as Benjamin's firstborn son. His sons are listed as Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah, Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram.

Shaharaim fathered children in the field of Moab after sending them away; Hushim and Baara were his wives. By Hodesh his wife he fathered Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Shachia, and Mirmah, and by Hushim he fathered Abitub and Elpaal.

Jerusalem is where the heads of fathers' households, chief men of the Benjamite lines descended from Elpaal, Beriah, Shimei, and Shashak, lived. The family of the father of Gibeon, including Mikloth's line, also lived there near their relatives.
Saul is traced in the line Ner, Kish, Saul. He became the father of Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal.

Chapter 9 records the genealogies of Israel and lists those who resettled in Jerusalem after Judah's captivity in Babylon. It names residents from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh, then the priests (1,760 able men) and Levites who lived there. A long section details the gatekeepers, 212 chosen ones descended from the Korahites, whom David and Samuel ordained, and their duties guarding the gates, rooms, treasuries, vessels, and provisions of God's house. The chapter also mentions the singers who lived in the rooms and worked day and night, and closes by repeating the Benjamite line of Jeiel and Ner through Saul, Jonathan, and Merib-baal down to Azel's six sons.

All Israel was listed by genealogies written in the book of the kings of Israel. The first inhabitants in their own possessions and cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants, while Judah had been carried captive to Babylon for disobedience.

Jerusalem was home to people of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh, along with priests, Levites, and gatekeepers. The heads of the Levite fathers' households and the Benjamite family of Jeiel's relatives also lived there.

The priests named include Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin, Azariah (ruler of God's house), Adaiah, and Maasai. Their brothers, heads of fathers' houses, numbered 1,760 very able men for the service of God's house, and some priests' sons prepared the mixing of the spices.

Levites listed include Shemaiah, Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal, Mattaniah, Obadiah, and Berechiah, some living in the Netophathite villages. They served as gatekeepers, keepers of vessels and baked goods, and singers who lived in the rooms, free from other service and working day and night.

The gatekeepers Shallum (chief), Akkub, Talmon, Ahiman, and their brothers were Korahites who previously served at the king's gate eastward. Totaling 212, they were ordained by David and Samuel, guarded the gates on four sides, were relieved by brothers coming every seven days, and opened the house each morning.

God's house was guarded on the east, west, north, and south by gatekeepers who also oversaw its rooms and treasuries. Its vessels were counted in and out, and its furniture, fine flour, wine, oil, frankincense, spices, baked goods, and show bread each had appointed caretakers.

The Philistines fight Israel at Mount Gilboa, and the men of Israel flee and fall slain. The Philistines kill Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, and archers overtake Saul, who then falls on his own sword after his armor bearer refuses to kill him. The armor bearer also falls on his sword, and the Israelites abandon their cities to the Philistines. The Philistines strip Saul's body, take his head and armor, and display them in the houses of their gods and of Dagon. The valiant men of Jabesh Gilead retrieve the bodies of Saul and his sons, bury their bones, and fast seven days; the chapter explains that Saul died for his trespass against the LORD, who turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.

Saul is overtaken by archers in the battle and, after his armor bearer refuses to kill him, falls on his own sword to avoid being abused by the uncircumcised. The Philistines later strip his body, take his head and armor, and display them in the houses of their gods and of Dagon. His body is retrieved and buried by the men of Jabesh Gilead.

The Philistines fight Israel, pursue Saul and his sons, and kill Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua. They strip the slain, take Saul's head and armor, send word to their idols and people, place his armor in the house of their gods and fasten his head in the house of Dagon. They also come to live in the cities the Israelites abandon.

The men of Israel flee before the Philistines and fall slain on Mount Gilboa. After seeing that Saul and his sons are dead, the Israelites in the valley abandon their cities and flee, and the Philistines move into them.
Mount Gilboa is where the men of Israel fall slain and where Saul and his sons die. The Philistines find the fallen bodies of Saul and his sons there the next day.

Three sons of Saul, Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, are killed by the Philistines, who pursue hard after them. They die together with Saul, and their bodies are later taken by the valiant men of Jabesh Gilead and their bones buried under the oak in Jabesh.

All Jabesh Gilead hears what the Philistines did to Saul. In response its valiant men take the bodies of Saul and his sons, bring them to Jabesh, and bury their bones under the oak there; the people fast seven days.

l: valiant men of Jabesh Gilead, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: The valiant men of Jabesh Gilead arise and take away the bodies of Saul and his sons. They bring them to Jabesh, bury their bones under the oak, and fast seven days.

The LORD is identified as the one against whom Saul trespassed by not keeping his word and by seeking counsel from a familiar spirit rather than inquiring of him. The text says the LORD killed Saul and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.
David, the son of Jesse, is named as the one to whom the LORD turns the kingdom over after Saul's death. He is not otherwise present in this unit.

l: Battle at Mount Gilboa, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: The battle goes against Israel as the Philistines put its men to flight and many fall slain on Mount Gilboa. Saul's three sons are killed, Saul is distressed by the archers, and the Israelites in the valley afterward abandon their cities.

Saul dies by falling on his own sword after his armor bearer, terrified, refuses to thrust him through. The armor bearer then also falls on his sword and dies, and Saul dies with his three sons and all his house together. The Philistines mutilate and display his body parts, while Jabesh Gilead later buries his bones.

The text states that Saul died for his trespass against the LORD, because he did not keep the LORD's word. It also says he asked counsel of one who had a familiar spirit and did not inquire of the LORD.

All Israel gathers to David at Hebron, affirms he is their bone and flesh, and with the elders anoints him king after he makes a covenant with them before the LORD. David and Israel then go to Jerusalem (Jebus), where the Jebusites taunt him, but he takes the stronghold of Zion, which becomes David's city; Joab goes up first and is made chief. David grows greater because the LORD of Armies is with him. The chapter then lists David's mighty men, including Jashobeam, Eleazar, Abishai, and Benaiah, and recounts how three of them broke through the Philistine army to draw water from the well of Bethlehem for David, who poured it out to the LORD rather than drink it. A long roster of further mighty men closes the chapter.

David is gathered to by all Israel at Hebron, makes a covenant with the elders, and is anointed king over Israel according to the LORD's word by Samuel. He takes the stronghold of Zion, lives there, and grows greater because the LORD of Armies is with him. When three mighty men bring him water from the well of Bethlehem, he refuses to drink it and pours it out to the LORD, calling it the blood of men who risked their lives.

All Israel gathers to David at Hebron, calling themselves his bone and flesh and recalling that he led them out and in even under Saul. Its elders anoint him king, and Israel goes with him to Jerusalem. The mighty men helped make him king together with all Israel according to the LORD's word concerning Israel.
Hebron is the place where all Israel and its elders come to David. There David makes a covenant with them before the LORD and they anoint him king.

The LORD is said to have told David he would shepherd and be prince over Israel, and David is anointed according to the LORD's word by Samuel. David grows greater because the LORD of Armies is with him, and the LORD saves the men at Pasdammim by a great victory. David pours out the water from Bethlehem to the LORD.

Jerusalem, also called Jebus, is where David and all Israel go after the anointing. Its inhabitants, the Jebusites, are there, and David takes the stronghold of Zion, which becomes David's city. David lives there, and the city is built around from Millo, with Joab repairing the rest.
The Jebusites are the inhabitants of the land at Jebus. They tell David he will not come in, but David nevertheless takes the stronghold of Zion.

Joab the son of Zeruiah goes up first against the Jebusites and is made chief, as David had promised to whoever struck them first. He repairs the rest of the city. He is also named as the brother of Abishai and of Asahel, and Naharai the Berothite is his armor bearer.

l: mighty men of David, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: The mighty men are listed as those who showed themselves strong with David in his kingdom and with all Israel to make him king. The chapter names Jashobeam, chief of the thirty, Eleazar, Abishai, Benaiah, and a long roster of others, including Uriah the Hittite, with their origins and some of their deeds.

The three mighty men break through the Philistine army to draw water from the well of Bethlehem and bring it to David, who will not drink it. Abishai is chief of the three but not included among them, and Benaiah gains a name among them but does not attain to them. Jashobeam and Eleazar are also named as among the leading mighty men.

The Philistines gather to battle at Pasdammim, where the people flee until Eleazar and others defend the barley plot and kill them. They are encamped in the valley of Rephaim and hold a garrison in Bethlehem, which the three break through to fetch water for David.
Bethlehem has a Philistine garrison at the time David longs for water from its well by the gate. Elhanan the son of Dodo is listed as being from Bethlehem.
The well of Bethlehem, by the gate, is what David longs to drink from. Three mighty men break through the Philistine army to draw its water, but David pours it out to the LORD instead of drinking it.

Benaiah, son of Jehoiada and of a valiant man of Kabzeel, killed the two sons of Ariel of Moab, a lion in a pit on a snowy day, and a five-cubit Egyptian whom he killed with the Egyptian's own spear. He had a name among the three and was more honorable than the thirty but did not attain to the three. David set him over his guard.
David makes a covenant with all the elders of Israel at Hebron before the LORD. After it, they anoint him king over Israel according to the LORD's word by Samuel.

David and all Israel go to Jebus, where the inhabitants tell him he will not come in, yet he takes the stronghold of Zion, which becomes David's city. Joab goes up first and is made chief, as David had promised. David then lives in the stronghold and builds the city around it.

Chapter 12 lists the warriors who joined David while he was a fugitive from Saul at Ziklag and in the wilderness stronghold. These included skilled archers and slingers from Saul's own tribe of Benjamin, lion-faced Gadite captains, men of Judah and Benjamin whom David tested and whom Amasai pledged to him, and Manasseh captains who helped him against raiders. The chapter then gives tribal troop counts of those who came armed to Hebron to turn Saul's kingdom to David according to the LORD's word, among them Judah, Simeon, Levi, Ephraim, Issachar, Zebulun, Naphtali, Dan, Asher and the tribes east of the Jordan. All came with a whole heart to make David king over all Israel. They feasted with him three days on provisions that neighboring tribes brought in abundance, for there was joy in Israel.

David was a fugitive from Saul at Ziklag and in the stronghold, where mighty men from many tribes came to help him until his force was like God's army. He tested the Benjamin and Judah arrivals, welcomed them after Amasai's pledge, and was made king over all Israel at Hebron, where he feasted three days.

Saul is the one David fled from, the son of Kish. Benjamin, his own relatives, supplied archers and slingers to David, though most of them had kept allegiance to Saul's house until then. The Philistine lords also feared David might desert to his master Saul, and the people came to Hebron to turn Saul's kingdom to David.

Hebron is where the armed men of the tribes gathered to turn Saul's kingdom to David according to the LORD's word. They came with a perfect heart to make David king over all Israel and stayed with him three days, eating and drinking.

Benjamin, Saul's own tribe, gave David archers and slingers who could use either hand, and some Benjamites came to him at the stronghold. At Hebron three thousand of them came, since most had until then kept their allegiance to Saul's house.

Some of Judah came with Benjamin to David at the stronghold, where David questioned their intent and Amasai pledged loyalty. At Hebron six thousand eight hundred of Judah bore shield and spear and armed for war.

Some Gadites joined David in the wilderness stronghold as mighty men of valor trained for war, with faces like lions and swiftness like gazelles. Eleven are named in order, from Ezer the chief to Machbannai, as army captains, the least equal to a hundred and the greatest to a thousand. They crossed the overflowing Jordan in the first month and put valley dwellers to flight.

Some of Manasseh joined David as he went to Ziklag after the Philistine lords sent him away from the battle against Saul. Seven named captains of thousands helped him against the band of raiders. At Hebron eighteen thousand of the half-tribe came to make David king, and the eastern half was included in the one hundred twenty thousand across the Jordan.

All Israel's tribes sent armed men to Hebron to make David king, and the rest of Israel was also of one heart. Issachar's leaders understood the times and knew what Israel ought to do. Neighbors from Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali brought abundant food, for there was joy in Israel.

David's army grew day by day as men came to help him until it was a great army like God's army. Its tribal contingents at Hebron are numbered, including Simeon seven thousand one hundred, Levi four thousand six hundred, Ephraim twenty thousand eight hundred, Zebulun fifty thousand, Naphtali thirty-seven thousand with a thousand captains, Dan twenty-eight thousand six hundred, Asher forty thousand, and one hundred twenty thousand from east of the Jordan.

l: feast at Hebron (David's coronation), 1 Chronicles, Chapter 12
s: After the tribes came to make David king, they stayed with him three days eating and drinking on provisions their brothers supplied. Those from as far as Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali brought flour, fig cakes, raisins, wine, oil, cattle and sheep on donkeys, camels, mules and oxen in abundance, for there was joy in Israel.

David consults the leaders of Israel and proposes, with the assembly's approval, to bring God's ark back because it was not sought in the days of Saul. He gathers all Israel and goes to Baalah, also called Kiriath Jearim, to fetch the ark. The ark is carried on a new cart from Abinadab's house, driven by Uzza and Ahio, while David and all Israel celebrate with music. At Chidon's threshing floor, Uzza puts out his hand to steady the ark when the oxen stumble, and the LORD strikes him dead. Afraid, David names the place Perez Uzza and diverts the ark to Obed-Edom the Gittite's house, where it stays three months and the LORD blesses that household.

David consulted Israel's leaders and proposed bringing the ark back, since it was not sought in Saul's days, and he led all Israel to Kiriath Jearim to fetch it. He played music before God, was displeased when the LORD struck Uzza, and named the place Perez Uzza. Afraid of God, he asked how he could bring the ark home and left it in Obed-Edom's house instead of taking it into David's city.

The ark, which sits above the cherubim and is called by the Name, was carried from Abinadab's house on a new cart toward David's city. When the oxen stumbled and Uzza touched it, the LORD struck Uzza dead. It was then diverted to Obed-Edom the Gittite's house, where it remained three months.

Uzza, with Ahio, drove the cart carrying the ark. At Chidon's threshing floor he put out his hand to hold the ark when the oxen stumbled, and the LORD's anger burned against him so that he died there before God. The place was called Perez Uzza.

The LORD's anger burned against Uzza for putting his hand on the ark, and he struck him dead, breaking out against him. He later blessed Obed-Edom's house and all that Obed-Edom had while the ark stayed there three months.

All the assembly of Israel agreed to David's plan because it seemed right to all the people. David assembled all Israel from the Shihor River of Egypt to the entrance of Hamath, and they went up with him and played before God with songs and instruments.
Obed-Edom the Gittite received the ark of God into his house when David would not move it to David's city. It stayed with his family three months, and the LORD blessed his house and all that he had.
Kiriath Jearim, also called Baalah, belonged to Judah and was where the ark was kept in Abinadab's house. David and all Israel went there to bring the ark up on a new cart.

Hiram king of Tyre sends messengers to David with cedar trees, masons, and carpenters to build him a house, and David perceives that the LORD has established him as king over Israel. David takes more wives in Jerusalem and fathers more children, whose names are listed. When the Philistines go up to seek David after he is anointed king over all Israel, he inquires of God and is told to go up, and he defeats them at Baal Perazim, burning their abandoned gods. When the Philistines raid the valley again, God directs David to circle around and attack opposite the mulberry trees at the sound of marching, and David strikes the Philistine army from Gibeon to Gezer. David's fame spreads into all lands, and the LORD brings fear of him on all nations.

David receives cedar, masons, and carpenters from Hiram king of Tyre to build his house, and he perceives that the LORD has established him as king over Israel. He takes more wives in Jerusalem and fathers more sons and daughters, including Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. He twice inquires of God before fighting the Philistines, obeys the instructions given, defeats them at Baal Perazim and from Gibeon to Gezer, and becomes famous in all lands.

The LORD is said to have established David as king over Israel, and he answers David's inquiry by telling him to go up against the Philistines and promising to deliver them into his hand. He brings the fear of David on all nations.

God is inquired of by David twice about the Philistines. The first time he says to go up and promises deliverance, and the second time he tells David not to go up directly but to come on them opposite the mulberry trees and go out to battle when he hears the sound of marching in the treetops. He declares that he has gone out before David to strike the Philistine army, and David credits him with breaking his enemies by his hand like waters breaking out.

Israel is the kingdom over which the LORD has established David, whose kingdom is highly exalted for his people Israel's sake. The Philistines go up to seek David after he is anointed king over all Israel.

The Philistines go up to seek David when they hear he is anointed king over all Israel, and they raid the valley of Rephaim. David defeats them at Baal Perazim, and they leave their gods there, which are burned with fire. They raid the valley again and their army is struck from Gibeon to Gezer.
Baal Perazim is the place where David and his men come up and defeat the Philistines. It receives its name because David says God has broken his enemies by his hand like waters breaking out.

David builds houses in David's city and prepares a tent for God's ark, declaring that only the Levites may carry it. He assembles all Israel at Jerusalem and gathers the sons of Aaron and the Levite family heads, including Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab, along with the priests Zadok and Abiathar, telling them to sanctify themselves because the LORD's earlier anger came from not seeking him according to the ordinance. The Levites carry the ark on their shoulders with poles as Moses commanded, while David has Levite singers and instrumentalists appointed, led by Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, with Chenaniah over the singing and priests blowing trumpets. David, the elders, and the captains bring the ark up from the house of Obed-Edom with joy, sacrificing seven bulls and seven rams, and all Israel shouts and sounds instruments. As the ark enters David's city, Michal the daughter of Saul looks from a window, sees king David dancing and playing, and despises him in her heart.

David prepared a place and a tent for God's ark and insisted that only the Levites carry it. He assembled Israel and the Levite leaders, told them to sanctify themselves, and had singers appointed. He went with the elders and captains to bring the ark up with joy, dressed in fine linen and a linen ephod, and was seen dancing and playing by Michal, who despised him.

The ark was given a prepared place and a tent in David's city, and was to be carried only by the Levites. The Levites bore it on their shoulders with poles, as Moses commanded, and it was brought up from the house of Obed-Edom to David's city amid sacrifices, music, and shouting.

The LORD is said to have chosen the Levites to carry his ark and minister to him forever. David states that the LORD broke out in anger against Israel earlier because they did not seek him according to the ordinance. He is also said to have helped the Levites who bore the ark of his covenant.

The Levites are named as the only ones who ought to carry the ark, and their family heads Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab were gathered with their brothers. They sanctified themselves and bore the ark on their shoulders with poles. Some were appointed as singers, instrumentalists, and doorkeepers, and they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams when God helped them.

All Israel was assembled at Jerusalem by David to bring up the ark. Together with the elders and captains over thousands, they brought the ark up with joy, shouting, and the sound of cornet, trumpets, cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps.

David directed the Levite chiefs to appoint singers with stringed instruments, harps, and cymbals to sound aloud with joy. Heman, Asaph, and Ethan were given bronze cymbals, others played stringed instruments set to Alamoth and harps tuned to the eight-stringed lyre, and Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, taught them because he was skillful. They wore fine linen robes in the procession.
Michal, the daughter of Saul, looked out at a window as the ark came into David's city. She saw king David dancing and playing, and she despised him in her heart.

l: procession bringing the ark up to Jerusalem, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 15
s: The procession carried the ark up from the house of Obed-Edom to David's city with David, the elders, and the captains over thousands, after the Levites had sanctified themselves. Seven bulls and seven rams were sacrificed, priests blew trumpets, and all Israel sounded cornets, trumpets, cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps with shouting. It ended with the ark's arrival in David's city, where Michal watched from a window.

The ark of God is brought into the tent David pitched for it, and David offers burnt offerings and peace offerings, blesses the people in the LORD's name, and gives every Israelite bread, meat, and a raisin cake. He appoints Levites, with Asaph as chief, to minister before the ark with instruments, while priests Benaiah and Jahaziel blow trumpets continually. On that day David first ordains a song of thanksgiving through Asaph and his brothers, which calls Israel to seek, remember, and praise the LORD for his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and calls all the earth to worship him as creator above idols. The people say "Amen" and praise the LORD. David leaves Asaph and his brothers at the ark, places Obed-Edom and others as doorkeepers, and stations Zadok and the priests at the tabernacle at Gibeon for daily offerings, with Heman and Jeduthun also giving thanks. Then everyone goes home and David returns to bless his house.

David has the ark set in the tent he pitched, offers burnt and peace offerings, blesses the people in the LORD's name, and distributes bread, meat, and a raisin cake to all Israel. He appoints Levites to minister before the ark, first ordains giving thanks to the LORD through Asaph and his brothers, and arranges ongoing service at the ark and at Gibeon. He then returns to bless his house.

The LORD is praised in the thanksgiving song as the God of Israel who keeps his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, protected the patriarchs and reproved kings for their sake, and is great and to be feared above all gods. He made the heavens, comes to judge the earth, is good, and his loving kindness endures forever.

The ark is brought in and set in the middle of the tent David pitched for it. Offerings are made before God there, and Asaph and his brothers are left to minister before it continually, with trumpets sounding before the ark of the covenant.

Some Levites are appointed by David to minister before the LORD's ark and to commemorate, thank, and praise the LORD. Named ones play stringed instruments, harps, and cymbals, and others, including Obed-Edom, serve as doorkeepers, while Heman and Jeduthun and others chosen by name give thanks.

Asaph is the chief of the appointed Levites and sounds aloud with cymbals. David ordains the giving of thanks through him and his brothers, and leaves them before the ark to minister continually as each day's work requires.

Israel, described as the offspring of his servant and children of Jacob, receives food from David and is addressed in the song as the LORD's chosen ones who should remember his covenant and the land promised to them. The people say "Amen," praise the LORD, and then depart each to his house.

David offers burnt offerings and peace offerings before God when the ark is placed in the tent. Zadok and the priests are also assigned to offer burnt offerings continually, morning and evening, on the altar at the tabernacle in Gibeon according to the LORD's law.

On that day David first ordains giving thanks to the LORD through Asaph and his brothers, and the song is recorded in this chapter. It urges calling on the LORD, remembering his wonders and covenant, declaring his glory among the nations, and recognizing that the LORD made the heavens while other gods are idols. It ends with a petition for deliverance, a blessing of the LORD, and the people's "Amen."

David tells Nathan the prophet that he lives in a cedar house while the ark of the LORD's covenant sits in a tent, and Nathan at first tells him to do all that is in his heart. That night God sends Nathan to tell David he will not build a house for the LORD, who has gone from tent to tent and never asked any judge of Israel for a cedar house. The LORD recounts taking David from the sheep pen to be prince over Israel, promises to make his name great, to plant Israel securely in its own place, and to build David a house. He promises to set up David's offspring after him, who will build the LORD's house and have a throne established forever, with the LORD as his father and loving kindness never taken from him. David sits before the LORD and responds in prayer, marveling at the honor, praising the LORD's uniqueness and Israel's redemption from Egypt, and asking that the promise be established forever.

David observes that he lives in a cedar house while the ark of the LORD's covenant is in a tent, but is told through Nathan that he will not build the LORD a house. He is reminded that the LORD took him from the sheep pen to be prince over Israel and promised him a great name and a house. David responds by sitting before the LORD in humble prayer, praising him and asking that the promise be established forever.

Nathan the prophet first tells David to do all that is in his heart, since God is with him. That night the word of God comes to him, and he faithfully delivers to David the LORD's message and vision, which forbids David to build the house and promises David a house.

The LORD declares that he has not lived in a house since bringing Israel up, but has moved from tent to tent, and that he never asked any judge for a cedar house. He promises David a name, a secure place for Israel, victory over enemies, a house, and an offspring whose throne he will establish forever. David praises him as incomparable and as the God who redeemed Israel from Egypt.

Israel is described as the people the LORD commanded judges to shepherd and whom he will appoint a place, plant, and no longer let the children of wickedness waste. David says no nation is like Israel, whom God redeemed from Egypt, driving out nations before them, and made his own people forever.

David's wish to replace the tent for the ark with a house is declined, as the LORD says David shall not build him a house to dwell in. The LORD says that David's offspring will build the house for him instead.

The LORD promises that he will build David a house, which David receives with amazement, asking who he and his house are. David prays that the house be established and blessed forever before the LORD, so that the name of the LORD may be magnified.

The LORD promises to set up one of David's sons after him when David goes to be with his fathers, and to establish his kingdom. This son will build the LORD a house, have his throne established forever, and be treated as a son by the LORD, who will not take his loving kindness from him as he did from the one before David. The text does not name him.

The LORD, through Nathan, promises David a house, an offspring to succeed him, and a throne and kingdom established forever, along with an enduring fatherly relationship. David accepts the promise in prayer, saying it gave him courage to pray, and asks that it be established forever as spoken, noting that the LORD has blessed the house and it is blessed forever.

David defeats the Philistines, taking Gath and its towns, and subdues Moab, which then pays tribute. He defeats Hadadezer king of Zobah, capturing chariots, horsemen, footmen, gold shields, and much bronze, and strikes the Syrians of Damascus who come to help Hadadezer, then garrisons Syria. Tou king of Hamath sends his son Hadoram with gifts of gold, silver, and bronze, and David dedicates these and other spoils from many nations to the LORD. Abishai the son of Zeruiah strikes eighteen thousand Edomites and garrisons Edom. The chapter closes by noting that David reigned over all Israel with justice and listing his officials: Joab, Jehoshaphat, Zadok, Abimelech, Shavsha, Benaiah, and David's sons.

David defeats the Philistines, Moab, Hadadezer king of Zobah, and the Syrians of Damascus, taking Gath, tribute, chariots, gold shields, and bronze, and he puts garrisons in Syria. He dedicates the silver, gold, and vessels from Hamath and from many nations to the LORD, and he reigns over all Israel, executing justice and righteousness for all his people.
The Philistines are defeated and subdued by David, who takes Gath and its towns from their hand. Some of the silver and gold David later dedicates to the LORD came from them.
Moab is defeated by David, and the Moabites become his servants and bring tribute. Silver and gold taken from Moab are among the spoils David dedicates to the LORD.

Hadadezer, king of Zobah, is defeated by David while David is going to establish his dominion by the river Euphrates, and loses one thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen. David takes the gold shields of his servants and much bronze from his cities Tibhath and Cun. Hadadezer had been at war with Tou king of Hamath, who sends greetings to David after the defeat.

The Syrians of Damascus come to help Hadadezer, and David strikes twenty-two thousand of their men. David then puts garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians become his servants and bring tribute.

The LORD gives victory to David wherever he goes, a statement made after the Syrian campaign and again after the Edom campaign. David dedicates to the LORD the vessels, silver, and gold taken from Hamath and from many nations.

Abishai the son of Zeruiah strikes eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. He puts garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites become servants to David; silver and gold from Edom are also among the spoils David dedicates to the LORD.

After Nahash king of the Ammonites died, David sent messengers to comfort his son Hanun, but Ammonite princes persuaded Hanun that they were spies, and he shaved them and cut off their garments before sending them away. David told the humiliated men to wait at Jericho until their beards grew back. Realizing they had made themselves odious to David, the Ammonites hired chariots and horsemen with a thousand talents of silver from Mesopotamia, Aram-maacah, and Zobah. Joab led Israel's army, splitting it with his brother Abishai, and both the Syrians and the Ammonites fled. When the Syrians regrouped under Shophach, David crossed the Jordan and defeated them, killing Shophach, after which Hadadezer's servants made peace with David and served him.

Hanun succeeded his father Nahash as king of the Ammonites and received David's messengers of comfort. Believing his princes' warning that they were spies, he shaved them, cut off their garments at the buttocks, and sent them away. He and the Ammonites then sent a thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen.

David chose to show kindness to Hanun because Hanun's father had shown kindness to him, and sent messengers to comfort him. After the servants were humiliated, he told them to stay at Jericho until their beards grew, and sent Joab against the Ammonites and their hirelings. He later gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, defeated the Syrians, killing seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand footmen along with Shophach, and received the submission of Hadadezer's servants.

The Ammonite princes convinced Hanun that David's comforters were spies, leading to the humiliation of David's servants. Seeing they had become odious to David, the Ammonites hired foreign forces and gathered from their cities for battle at the city gate. They fled before Abishai when the Syrians fled, retreating into their city, and were left without Syrian help after Hadadezer's servants made peace with David.

David's servants went to Hanun in the land of the Ammonites to comfort him over his father's death. They were shaved and had their garments cut off at the buttocks, then sent away greatly humiliated. David told them to stay at Jericho until their beards had grown, and then return.

Joab was sent by David with the whole army of mighty men. Facing battle lines before and behind, he took choice men of Israel against the Syrians and gave the rest to his brother Abishai against the Ammonites, urging courage and trust in the LORD's will. The Syrians fled before him, and he then came to Jerusalem.

Israel's army, led by Joab and Abishai, put both the Syrians and the Ammonites to flight. When the Syrians regathered, all Israel under David crossed the Jordan and defeated them. As a result the Syrians made peace with David and served him.

The Syrians fled before Joab and later called out more Syrians from beyond the River under Shophach, captain of Hadadezer's army. David defeated them, killing seven thousand charioteers, forty thousand footmen, and Shophach. Hadadezer's servants then made peace with David, served him, and would no longer help the Ammonites.

l: mercenary force (hired by Ammon), 1 Chronicles, Chapter 19
s: Hanun and the Ammonites sent a thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, Aram-maacah, and Zobah. The text says they hired thirty-two thousand chariots and the king of Maacah with his people, who camped near Medeba. The hired forces were stationed in the field apart from the Ammonites and fled when Joab advanced.

l: war between Israel and Ammon/Syrians, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 19
s: The war began after Hanun humiliated David's servants and the Ammonites hired Syrian forces. Joab and Abishai routed the Syrians and Ammonites at the city gate, and David later defeated a second Syrian force under Shophach after crossing the Jordan. It ended in Syrian submission to David and the withdrawal of Syrian support from Ammon.

At the season when kings go out to war, Joab led the army against the children of Ammon, wasted their country, besieged Rabbah, and overthrew it, while David stayed at Jerusalem. David took the Ammonite king's golden, jewel-set crown, which was placed on his own head, carried off much plunder, and had the people of the city cut with saws, iron picks, and axes, doing the same to all the Ammonite cities before returning to Jerusalem. Wars with the Philistines followed: Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Sippai, Elhanan the son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath, and Jonathan the son of Shimea, David's brother, killed a man of great stature at Gath with twenty-four fingers and toes. The chapter closes by stating that these giants born in Gath fell by the hand of David and his servants.
Joab led out the army at the time when kings go out, wasted the country of the children of Ammon, and besieged Rabbah. He struck Rabbah and overthrew it.

David stayed at Jerusalem while Joab fought at Rabbah, then took the Ammonite king's crown, which weighed a talent of gold and held precious stones, and had it set on his own head. He brought out much plunder and had the people cut with saws, iron picks, and axes, doing so to all the Ammonite cities, before returning to Jerusalem. The giants born in Gath are said to have fallen by his hand and the hands of his servants.

The children of Ammon had their country wasted by Joab's army, and their cities were treated as Rabbah's people were. Their king's crown was taken by David, and the people of their cities were cut with saws, iron picks, and axes.
Rabbah was besieged by Joab, struck, and overthrown. David took the king's crown, much plunder, and the people from the city.

The Philistines fought Israel in wars at Gezer and Gath and in another unnamed engagement. In these wars their giants, including Sippai, Lahmi, and the man of great stature, were killed by Israelite warriors.
In the war with the Philistines at Gezer, Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Sippai, of the sons of the giant. The Philistine giants there were subdued.

l: Elhanan the son of Jair, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: In another war with the Philistines, Elhanan the son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite. Lahmi's spear had a staff like a weaver's beam.

l: man of great stature (at Gath), 1 Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: At a war at Gath, this man of great stature had twenty-four fingers and toes, six on each hand and six on each foot, and was born to the giant. He defied Israel and was killed by Jonathan the son of Shimea.

l: Jonathan the son of Shimea, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: Jonathan, identified as David's brother and the son of Shimea, killed the man of great stature at Gath when he defied Israel.
The text says certain men were born to the giant in Gath, including Sippai, Lahmi, and the six-fingered man. All of them fell by the hand of David and his servants.

l: war with the Philistines, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: Three engagements are recorded: at Gezer, where Sibbecai killed Sippai; another where Elhanan killed Lahmi; and at Gath, where Jonathan killed a man of great stature. Each ended with a giant of the Philistines slain, and the first is said to have ended with the Philistines subdued.

Satan moves David to order a census of Israel, and David sends Joab to count the people despite Joab's protest that it will bring guilt on Israel. Joab reports 1,100,000 swordsmen in Israel and 470,000 in Judah, omitting Levi and Benjamin, and God, displeased, strikes Israel. David confesses his sin, and through the seer Gad the LORD offers him three punishments; David chooses to fall into the LORD's hand, and a pestilence kills seventy thousand men. As the LORD's angel is about to destroy Jerusalem, the LORD relents, and David pleads that the punishment fall on himself and his house rather than on the people. At the angel's command David buys Ornan the Jebusite's threshing floor for six hundred shekels of gold, builds an altar, and offers sacrifices, and the LORD answers by fire and has the angel sheathe his sword.

David, moved by Satan, orders a census of Israel over Joab's objection, then confesses that he has sinned greatly and acted foolishly. He chooses to fall into the LORD's hand rather than man's, pleads that the punishment fall on himself and his father's house instead of the people, and buys Ornan's threshing floor at full price, refusing to offer a sacrifice that costs him nothing. He builds an altar there and the LORD answers him by fire, though he is too afraid of the angel's sword to go to the tabernacle at Gibeon.
Satan stands up against Israel and moves David to take a census of Israel. He appears only at the start of the chapter, as the instigator of the census.
Israel is counted at 1,100,000 men who draw a sword, with Judah counted at 470,000. Because of the census God strikes Israel, and seventy thousand of its men fall in the pestilence.

Joab protests the census, asking why David would cause guilt for Israel, but the king's word prevails and he carries it out across Israel. He reports the totals to David, leaving out Levi and Benjamin because the king's word was abominable to him.

The LORD, displeased with the census, strikes Israel, and through Gad offers David a choice of three punishments. He sends a pestilence, relents when the angel is about to destroy Jerusalem, and tells the angel to withdraw his hand. He directs David to raise an altar at Ornan's threshing floor, answers David by fire from the sky, and commands the angel to sheathe his sword.

Gad is identified as David's seer and brings the LORD's offer of three punishments to David. He later passes on the angel's command that David build an altar on Ornan's threshing floor, and David goes up at his word.

Ornan is threshing wheat when he sees the angel, and his four sons hide. He bows to David and offers the threshing floor, oxen, threshing instruments and wheat free, but David insists on paying, and Ornan receives six hundred shekels of gold for the place.

The LORD's angel destroys in the pestilence and is sent to Jerusalem, but the LORD tells him to withdraw his hand as he is about to destroy it. David sees him standing between earth and sky with a drawn sword over Jerusalem, and he commands Gad to tell David to raise an altar. After David's sacrifice the angel puts his sword back into its sheath.

The census is instigated by Satan and ordered by David from Beersheba to Dan, and is carried out by Joab, who counts 1,100,000 swordsmen in Israel and 470,000 in Judah but omits Levi and Benjamin. It displeases God and brings the strike on Israel, and David acknowledges it as his sin.

The pestilence is the third option the LORD offers, three days of the sword of the LORD with the angel destroying throughout Israel's borders, and David chooses it. Seventy thousand men of Israel fall before the LORD relents and the plague is stopped.

l: threshing floor of Ornan, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: The threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite is where the LORD's angel stands when the LORD relents from destroying Jerusalem. David buys it for six hundred shekels of gold as the site for an altar, so that the plague may be stopped.

l: altar (David's altar to the LORD), 1 Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: At the angel's command David builds an altar on Ornan's threshing floor and offers burnt offerings and peace offerings there. The LORD answers him from the sky by fire on the altar, and David sacrifices there, while the tabernacle and its altar of burnt offering remain at the high place at Gibeon.

l: three choices of punishment, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: Through Gad the LORD offers David three years of famine, three months of being consumed before his foes while their sword overtakes him, or three days of the LORD's sword in a pestilence with the angel destroying throughout Israel. David chooses to fall into the LORD's hand because his mercies are very great, rather than into man's hand.

David declares the site to be the house of the LORD God and the altar of burnt offering for Israel, then gathers foreigners and masons and stockpiles iron, bronze, cedar, gold, and silver for the temple because his son Solomon is young and tender. He summons Solomon and tells him that the LORD forbade David to build the house because he had shed much blood in great wars. The LORD promised a peaceful son named Solomon who would build the house, be God's son, and have his throne established over Israel forever. David charges Solomon to keep the law, be strong and courageous, and begin the work with the abundant materials and skilled workmen provided. He also commands Israel's princes to help Solomon and to bring the ark of the covenant and holy vessels into the new house.

David declares the site the house of the LORD God and the altar of burnt offering, and gathers foreigners and masons and prepares abundant materials before his death. He tells Solomon that the LORD barred him from building because he shed much blood, then charges Solomon to build and commands Israel's princes to help him.

Solomon is described by David as young and tender, and is called and commanded to build a house for the LORD. He is told of the LORD's promise that he will be a man of peace, God's son, and that his throne over Israel will be established forever. David urges him to keep the law, be strong and courageous, and arise and act.

The LORD God had told David he could not build the house because of the blood he shed, and promised a son named Solomon who would build it and receive peace and quiet for Israel. He is said to be with the princes, to have given Israel rest on every side, and to have delivered the land's inhabitants into David's hand.

The house is to be built for the LORD's name, exceedingly magnificent and of fame and glory throughout all countries. David declares the site to be the house of the LORD God, and it is to receive the ark of the covenant and the holy vessels. Solomon is appointed to build it, though David had wanted to.

Israel is the people for whom the altar of burnt offering stands and over whom Solomon's throne will be established forever. The LORD promises peace and quietness to Israel in Solomon's days. Its princes are commanded to help Solomon, and its land is described as subdued before the LORD and his people.

David prepared iron for nails and couplings, bronze without weight, and cedar without number brought by the Sidonians and people of Tyre. He also prepared one hundred thousand talents of gold, one million talents of silver, and timber and stone, with skilled workmen in abundance. Solomon is told he may add to them.

In old age David makes his son Solomon king over Israel and assembles the princes, priests, and Levites. The Levites aged thirty and up are counted at thirty-eight thousand, and David assigns them to oversee the LORD's house, serve as officers and judges, act as doorkeepers, and praise the LORD with instruments. They are divided by the three sons of Levi, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, with the family heads listed under each, including Aaron and Moses among the Kohathites. Aaron and his sons are set apart for the most holy things, incense, ministry, and blessing, while Moses's sons are counted among the tribe of Levi. Because the LORD has given rest to his people and dwells in Jerusalem, David's last words lower the counting age to twenty and the Levites no longer carry the tabernacle, instead assisting the sons of Aaron in the house's service, offerings, and daily praise.

David, old and full of days, made his son Solomon king over Israel and gathered Israel's princes, priests, and Levites. He had the Levites counted and divided into divisions and duties, and by his last words set the counting age at twenty and up since the LORD now dwelt in Jerusalem.
Solomon is made king over Israel by his father David, who is old and full of days.

The Levites aged thirty and up numbered thirty-eight thousand and were divided under Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Because the tabernacle no longer needed carrying, their duty became waiting on the sons of Aaron in the LORD's house, offering, and morning and evening thanks and praise.

The LORD, the God of Israel, is said by David to have given rest to his people and to dwell in Jerusalem forever. The Levites serve him through the work of his house, praise, and burnt offerings on Sabbaths, new moons, and set feasts.

Twenty-four thousand Levites were assigned to oversee the work of the LORD's house, and others served as officers, judges, doorkeepers, and musicians. The Levites served in its courts and rooms, in purifying holy things, and in preparing the show bread and meal offerings.

Aaron, a son of Amram of the Kohathites and brother of Moses, was separated with his sons forever to sanctify the most holy things. His role was to burn incense before the LORD, minister to him, and bless in his name.

The sons of Aaron were set apart forever with Aaron for the most holy things, incense, ministry, and blessing. The Levites were to wait on them for the service of the LORD's house and keep their duty.

The Levites aged thirty and up were counted at thirty-eight thousand by their polls, man by man. A further count by David's last words registered the heads of fathers' houses from twenty years old and upward, in the number of names.

l: Levite divisions and duties, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: David divided the Levites by the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, listing family heads under each, and assigned 24,000 to oversee the work, 6,000 as officers and judges, 4,000 as doorkeepers, and 4,000 as musicians. Their duties included service in the courts and rooms, purifying holy things, preparing show bread and offerings, standing morning and evening to thank and praise, and offering burnt offerings at the set times.

Chapter 24 records how David, with Zadok of the sons of Eleazar and Ahimelech of the sons of Ithamar, divided the sons of Aaron into twenty-four orders for priestly service. Nadab and Abihu died childless before their father, so only Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests; Eleazar's line had sixteen chief houses and Ithamar's eight. The divisions were assigned impartially by lot, recorded by the scribe Shemaiah the son of Nethanel before the king, the princes, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of the fathers' houses, with the lots running from Jehoiarib first to Maaziah twenty-fourth. The chapter then lists the remaining Levite houses, including descendants of Amram, Izhar, Hebron, Uzziel, and Merari. These too cast lots in the same way, the chief's house and the younger brother's house being treated alike.
Aaron is the father of Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. The ordering of priestly service is said to follow the ordinance he gave, as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded him.

The sons of Aaron are named as Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Nadab and Abihu died before their father without children, so only Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests, and the Levites cast lots like them.
Eleazar survived Nadab and Abihu and served as priest. His descendants had more chief men than Ithamar's, sixteen heads of fathers' houses, and Zadok is of his line.
Ithamar served as priest along with Eleazar after his brothers died childless. His descendants had eight heads of fathers' houses, and Ahimelech is of his line.

David, with Zadok and Ahimelech, divided the sons of Eleazar and Ithamar according to their ordering in service. The lots were cast in his presence as king, both for the priests and for the other Levites.
Zadok, a priest of the sons of Eleazar, helped David divide the priests into their orders. He was present when Shemaiah recorded the lots and when the other Levites cast lots.

Ahimelech, of the sons of Ithamar and the son of Abiathar, helped David and Zadok divide the priests by their service. He was present before Shemaiah wrote down the lots and when the Levites cast lots.

The priests, descended from Eleazar and Ithamar, were divided into twenty-four orders by lot, sixteen from Eleazar's houses and eight from Ithamar's. Each order had its time to come into the LORD's house according to Aaron's ordinance.

The rest of the Levites are listed by house, including descendants of Amram, Izhar, Hebron, Uzziel, and Merari. They cast lots in the presence of David, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of the fathers' households, just as the sons of Aaron did. Shemaiah the son of Nethanel, a Levite, served as the scribe.

l: division of priestly service by lot, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: Twenty-four lots were drawn impartially, since there were princes of the sanctuary and of God in both Eleazar's and Ithamar's lines. The first lot fell to Jehoiarib, the second to Jedaiah, and so on to Maaziah, twenty-fourth, and Shemaiah recorded them before the king and leaders.

David and the captains of the army set apart certain sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to prophesy with harps, stringed instruments, and cymbals in the service of God's house. The chapter lists the sons of Asaph (four), Jeduthun (six), and Heman (fourteen, with three daughters), all serving under their fathers and under the king's order. Together with their brothers, the skilled and instructed singers numbered two hundred eighty-eight. They cast lots for their offices, with small and great, teacher and student treated alike. The lots produced twenty-four divisions, each of twelve sons and brothers, assigned in order from Joseph of Asaph's house to Romamti-Ezer.
David, with the captains of the army, set apart certain sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun for the service of prophesying with musical instruments. The musicians remained under the order of the king.
Asaph had four sons named: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asharelah, who served under his hand. Asaph prophesied at the order of the king, and the first lot fell to Joseph of his sons.

Jeduthun had six sons named: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Shimei, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, who served under his hands. He prophesied with the harp in giving thanks and praising the LORD, and he served under the king's order.
